Since 2010,
the Tate Modern in London
has devoted a gallery to Cy Twombly, the postwar American painter who died in 2011. In it are three large paintings from his “Bacchus” series — enormous abstract canvases of drippy red spirals dating from 2006-8 — along with five bronze sculptures and assemblages of found objects, such as the top of an olive barrel, that were made between 1979 and 1991.
“They were installed just as Cy had envisioned them,” said Nicholas Serota, director of all the Tate museums. This artist’s association with the Tate has been a long one, capped by a major retrospective there, titled “Cy Twombly: Cycles and Seasons” in 2008.
Recently Mr. Serota learned that, following the artist’s wishes, the Cy Twombly Foundation has donated all the works in that gallery to the Tate. “For us, it is the equivalent of gaining the Rothko Room,” Mr. Serota said, referring to a gallery of murals that Rothko had originally been commissioned to create for the Four Seasons Restaurant in New York, but which he ended up giving to the Tate in 1969. “And now, the Tate becomes one of the places in the world to see Cy Twombly,” along with the Menil Collection in Houston,
the Brandhorst Museum
in Munich and the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
Both the paintings and sculptures have their roots in ancient art. The Roman god Bacchus is a recurring theme in Twombly’s work, and his sculptures were created to evoke classical artifacts such as chariots and ships.
‘BIG BAMBÚ’ IN ISRAEL
As blockbusters go, “Big Bambú” — a giant labyrinthine jungle of bamboo with walking paths often rising some 50 feet in the air by the identical twin artists Mike and Doug Starn — is a guaranteed crowd-pleaser. More than 600,000 visitors trekked along the installation at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2010. Since then, variations of the project have been created in Venice on the Grand Canal next to the Peggy Guggenheim Collection, at the Museum of Modern Art in Rome and in the Naoshima Museum in Japan, where it is a permanent installation.
Next week, yet
another iteration of “Big Bambú”
will open in the art garden at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem. Called “5,000 Arms To Hold You,” it soars more than 52.5 feet, covers 7,500 square feet and consists of 10,000 bamboo poles, which took 25 rock climbers seven weeks, working 350 hours, to construct. “It’s our most elaborate one to date,” the twins said, talking at the same time during a telephone interview. “We call it a mansion with many rooms and pathways.”
“Big Bambú is all about interconnections,” they said. “And since Jerusalem is a city of three religions — Judaism, Christianity and Islam — we decided to bring Buddhism into the conversation.” They added that the title is a loose reference to the thousand-armed statue of Guanyin, the revered Buddhist figure. “We thought this might be a good place for some Buddhism, a spiritual neutral zone,” they said.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
As the project grows, the artists are recording it on their
website
. When “5,000 Arms to Hold You,” ends in October, not all will be lost. The tower in the shape of a double helix will become a permanent installation.
NATIONAL GALLERY GROWS
After a renovation and expansion that has closed the East Building of the
National Gallery of Art in Washington
for nearly three years, its reopening in the fall of 2016 will reveal not only more improved spaces but also a more comprehensive collection.
Little by little, curators there have been filling gaps. In the latest round of acquisitions, which were approved by the National Gallery’s board several weeks ago, it has added works by living artists in areas including Arte Povera and video.
Two of them — Michelangelo Pistoletto’s “
Donna che indica (Woman Who Points)
” from 1962/1982 and Barbara Kruger’s “Untitled (know nothing, believe anything, forget everything),” conceived in 1987 but made this year — are by artists the museum did not have in its collection until now. Harry Cooper, a curator who is the National Gallery’s head of contemporary art, explained that “when it comes to Arte Povera, we got a piece by Mario Merz last year, and now we have a signature late mirror painting by Pistoletto.” Depicting a woman pointing at a distant object that the viewer cannot see, it “blurs the boundaries between art and the spectator,” he said.
And, in an attempt to strengthen its representation of art from the 1980s that uses political language and ideology, the museum has added one of Ms. Kruger’s text pieces depicting a photograph of a woman receiving some sort of medical treatment to her eye. “It’s mysterious and disturbing,” Mr. Cooper said.
Other acquisitions include an accordion-fold book called “Portage (2000)” by the South African artist William Kentridge. Although the museum has two series of prints by him, it wanted to have a stronger representation in its holdings. “Portage” unfolds to nearly 14 feet long. He created the book by arranging small pieces of torn black paper into figures that were then glued onto pages from a French dictionary.
It also acquired “Street,” a video by the British-born artist James Nares that is already on view in the West Building’s Project Room, through July 6. To make it, Mr. Nares recorded 16 hours of footage of people on the streets of Manhattan from a moving car, which he then slowed down and edited into a 16-minute video of continuous motion. Sarah Greenough, the senior curator who heads the museum’s photography department, said that video is an area the National Gallery has begun to collect, and that “Street” is a perfect addition to its holdings, because it dovetails with its collection of street photography and urban imagery.
Acquisitions are not all that’s new at the National Gallery. It has also elected a new president, Frederick W. Beinecke, director of Antaeus Enterprises, a private investment company in New York. Mr. Beinecke, who has been on the museum’s board for seven years, is succeeding Victoria P. Sant, who had held the post since 2003.

Dear Diary:
Whack! I was slammed by the door of a parked car, flung open by a driver who was so proud of her primo parking spot on Amsterdam Avenue and 96th Street that she didn’t see me standing right outside her window.
I stumbled to the sidewalk, with an unpleasantly wet chin.   Something about that whack foretold the need for stitches and an uncomfortable session with a plastic surgeon. True, I had been standing near the car but in the street, hoping to hail a taxi. And true, I had been listening (with one ear only!) to “The Rosie Project,” an audiobook that had been making me laugh out loud for days.
The driver and her friend came to my side. They fumbled for tissues. “Can we get you a taxi?” the driver asked.  She did seem concerned. I said I lived in the neighborhood.  “Oh, she lives right here!” said the other.  “That’s great!  We can take her home.”
“But we just got this parking spot,” protested the driver.

LOS ANGELES — California’s plan to offer driver’s licenses to immigrants in the country illegally has hit a major snag, with the Obama administration informing state officials that the licenses they had designed violated federal law, California officials said Tuesday.
The problem: The proposed design makes the special licenses for immigrants look too much like regular driver’s licenses.
Last year, California became the most populous state to agree to issue driver’s licenses to undocumented residents, a move intended largely to keep the roads safer. But the state is now struggling to put the program into effect, with immigrants telling officials at
community meetings
that they feared the licenses would mark them as targets for police officers to turn over to immigration authorities, even though that is prohibited by state law.
Federal law passed after Sept. 11, 2001, requires any state licenses issued to unlawful residents to be easily distinguished from all forms of identification that could be used to board commercial airplanes. The
Department of Homeland Security
, which must approve the licenses, said in a letter to the California Department of Motor Vehicles that their design, which replaced the “DL” on the front of driver’s licenses with a “DP” for “Driving Privilege,” did not meet that standard.
The appearance of the new licenses has been one of the most contentious political questions facing California officials as they try to persuade the state’s estimated 2.5 million undocumented immigrants, many of whom harbor a deep mistrust of American government, to hand over their personal information to the state and get on the road legally.
State officials had hoped to quell such fears by making the distinction on the front of the license subtle, with a federal disclaimer on the back of the card. But that plan has now run afoul of federal regulators, who want to ensure that such a license would not fool a Transportation Security Administration agent glancing through hundreds of documents at an airport.
Immigration reform activists criticized the federal government’s interpretation of the law.
“We came up with this design, keeping in mind that immigrants continue to be very vulnerable, subject to discrimination, victims of crime and targets of scams,” said State Senator Ricardo Lara, chairman of the California Latino Legislative Caucus. “We don’t want to provide them with licenses that will open them up to further discrimination.”
Mr. Lara said the Department of Homeland Security’s decision threatened to delay California’s efforts to offer licenses to immigrants, which must begin by the start of next year under state law.
Several other states have already begun issuing driver’s licenses to unlawful residents. In Nevada, which began doing so this year, the front of the licenses says “Not Valid for Identification” just above “Driver Authorization Card.”
In the letter rejecting California’s design, Department of Homeland Security officials wrote that the license “must clearly state on the face and in the machine readable zone that it may not be accepted for federal purposes.”

Mariano Avnar and Yvon Rodriguez have put the band back together.
More than 10 years ago, Mr. Avnar and Ms. Rodriguez ran Patrias in Port Chester. He was the chef, she was the manager, and the menu featured dishes from their home countries, Spain (his) and Peru (hers). The name was fitting; in Spanish, “patrias” means homelands.
After they sold the restaurant, Mr. Avnar was the co-owner and chef of the Spanish spot
España
in Larchmont for seven years, until it closed in 2013.
Now Mr. Avnar and Ms. Rodriguez are presiding over a new edition of Patrias in New Rochelle, featuring some of their greatest hits: ceviches, tapas, paellas and lomo saltado, the Peruvian celebration of steak and starch.
It’s a small, cozy room, one wall of which is taken up by an oversize chalkboard menu that has the effect of enthusiastically announcing: Dig in.
So, begin with the silky, citrusy scallop ceviche in which the sea scallops are thinly sliced, carpaccio-style, along with an order of the delicate lamb meatballs in a pleasant curry sauce with diced carrots. Add to this a plate of the salt-cod fritters, crisp outside, creamy within, served with a robust roasted red pepper aioli.
If fried artichoke hearts are on the specials menu, get them. The light batter delivers a nice crunch, and they’re full of flavor; the aioli works very well with these too. Sautéed shrimp are straightforward — olive oil, garlic, a bit of heat from red chili pepper. And for pasta, there are the canelones, filled with a gently seasoned mixture of pork, chicken and veal and topped with a mild manchego sauce. It should be noted that I was the only person at the table who thoroughly enjoyed this dish, but then, I am categorically pro-cannelloni. (Not as winning was a mixed-seafood ceviche in which both the squid and the tomatoes were tough.)
Main courses are substantial and made for sharing. A tasty, triangle-shaped tuna steak is grilled as requested and accompanied by a bright tapenade with green olives. Tender baby lamb chops with garlicky sliced potatoes (patatas panaderas) may be, at $14, the best deal on the menu.
Paella has been a signature of Mr. Avnar’s at both the original Patrias and España, and it is also a popular attraction at his new place. His hearty seafood version is served in a pan with saffron-accented rice and an abundance of squid, shrimp, mussels, cuttlefish, bay scallops and clams.
Mr. Avnar also turns out an excellent lomo saltado: sautéed strips of beef, onions and tomato, a splash of soy sauce, with spears of skin-on fried potato in the mix and rice on the side. It would be an ideal dish to eat before or after you engage in several hours of vigorous log-splitting.
There is limited room in the kitchen, so only two desserts are made in-house: a homey flan with caramel sauce and a
crema catalana
that is something of a shrug. Mr. Avnar said other desserts, made with his recipes, are prepared by a baker he has hired; they include a flaky apple tart with vanilla ice cream that made a quick disappearance.
The Patrias wine list is compact but has a number of appealing bottles from Spain at modest prices; sangria is also on the list, as are soda-and-wine drinks like the calimocho, a Spanish-style red wine and Coca-Cola combo that tastes like, well, red wine mixed with Coke. (An optimist would hope that they bring out the best in each other. They don’t.)
Ms. Rodriguez seemed noticeably happy when she brought me that drink, and she is such a welcoming host that you hate to disappoint her (I dutifully finished most of it). She also has a good sense of humor. After explaining the meaning of some of the Incan symbols on one wall — condor included — she added that they were, in fact, stickers and then, with a laugh, offered that they cost $11. Good deal.
Also entertaining is the music on the sound system. There’s a lot of flamenco by Spanish singers like Estrella Morente and Montse Cortés, and an occasional song by a group like LoCura out of Northern California that blends flamenco with, among other sounds, Latin American rhythms.
Which, at Patrias, is perfect, really.

Inon Barnatan is ubiquitous this season. An Israeli-born New Yorker, Mr. Barnatan is the New York Philharmonic’s first “artist in association.” So he’s at the piano for a
chamber recital
with Philharmonic instrumentalists in December, and makes his full Philharmonic
debut
in March. He’s a guest artist with the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, with
a concert
in November. He’s
resident pianist
for the Jerusalem Quartet’s Brahms survey at the 92nd Street Y in October. And, lest downtown feel left out, he was the star attraction at SubCulture’s second PianoFest on Tuesday night.
Making oneself unmissable is one way to stand out in the ever-growing crowd of young pianists. But Mr. Barnatan, 35, offers much more. On Tuesday he demonstrated, in one of the most thoughtful and effective recitals I have heard from a pianist under 40, a sensitivity reminiscent of two other New York institutions, Emanuel Ax and Murray Perahia.
He also has a gift for programming. “Voices” was the theme of the concert at SubCulture’s basement space in Greenwich Village, as Mr. Barnatan explained. It was vague, perhaps, but it provided a useful thread through pieces that spanned three centuries of composition.
In several of them, multiple voices competed for attention. In Bach’s
Toccata in E minor
(BWV 914), its rhetorical sections given a grandeur rarely heard now, the fugue was agile and clear. Then there was Barber’s
Sonata in E flat minor
(Op. 26), a demanding work written for Vladimir Horowitz. Influences from Bach to jazz mingle in forms as old as the waltz and the passacaglia, all in a language that Mr. Barnatan’s playing emphasized could be gentle one moment and knotty another, yet always coherent.
Mendelssohn’s
Rondo Capriccioso
(Op. 14) seemed briefly to have a single voice, a bel canto line Mr. Barnatan floated as well as any soprano. Matthias Pintscher’s
“whirling tissue of light”
(2013), written for Mr. Barnatan, takes its title from Ezra Pound’s “Phanopoeia,” a poem about a poetic technique involving images cast on the visual imagination. The music flashes and shimmers in growling reds and icy violets, chased by a voice that interrupts and insists.
Franck’s
Prélude, Choral et Fugue
(Op. 21), its voices Bachian and Lisztian, organlike and orchestral, struck most. It was amply descriptive, so pungent that a listener could almost smell incense wafting down a nave. But crucially, Mr. Barnatan kept an uncommon, ideal balance between impulse and structural foresight, so that the concluding heap of themes, with bells pealing, carried transcendent, redemptive weight.

What is the textbook approach to leading against small slams and grand slams? Should you be aggressive or cautious?
In the diagramed deal, look at the West hand and the auction. What would you lead against seven spades?
The deal arose during the European Team Championships in Opatija, Croatia, last month. The winning England senior team’s nonplaying captain, Simon Cochemé suggested that this deal would be suitable for a column. It was also described in The Daily Bulletin by Marek Wojcicki, the coach of the Polish open team. The auction given was by Colin Simpson (North) and David Price (South) from the England senior team.
The deal was played in all three events: open, women’s and senior. These were the contracts reached (and how often): seven no-trump (four), seven spades (51), six no-trump (srven), six spades (17) and game (three).
Seven no-trump always failed, so let’s concentrate on seven spades. What should West lead?
It is normal to lead aggressively against a small slam, but passively against a grand slam. Here, though, whenever West chose a cautious lead, a heart or trump, the contract made. Declarer won in the dummy (say, with the heart ace), drew two rounds of trumps, cashed the club ace and ruffed a club. When the queen appeared, the contract was a claim. Declarer had six spades, three hearts, one diamond and three clubs. Note, though, that even if a defender had held queen-fourth of clubs, the contract would still have made. There were sufficient dummy entries to establish and cash the club jack.
At 14 tables, West found the demonic diamond-five lead, confident that the ace was in the dummy. Note that this removed a vital dummy entry for establishing the club suit by ruffing if a defender had queen-fourth and trumps were 4-1. Declarer cannot both take three heart tricks and establish and cash dummy’s clubs.
After this lead, eight declarers failed. Presumably, they either gambled on a 3-2 spade break (by cashing dummy’s ace and overtaking the jack with the king), or, after taking dummy’s two top trumps and seeing the bad break, they overtook dummy’s heart queen with their king, drew trumps and relied on the club finesse.
Price won with dummy’s diamond ace and cashed its two top trumps. Then he took the club ace and ruffed a club in his hand. When the queen appeared, he claimed. This line was duplicated by Krzysztof Lasocki of the Poland senior team and probably the other four successful declarers.
Mathematically, which is the better approach? Someone in Poland claims the winning line is 4 percent better than relying on the club finesse. But no one could work that out at the table. Occasionally, one just has to guess well.

Amy Sheng can sum up in one sentence why it’s important to have more female scientists and engineers designing products — especially if those products involve childbirth or breast-feeding. “A guy cannot fundamentally understand,” she said.
A Stanford-educated mechanical engineer, Ms. Sheng was reacting to recent efforts, including a
hackathon
that the Massachusetts Institute of Technology held in September to come up with a better breast pump. But the sentiment also applies to her own company’s invention, which is aimed chiefly at mothers.
Ms. Sheng is a co-founder of CellScope, a smartphone attachment that allows parents to take videos of a child’s middle ear that can be sent to doctors for an ear-infection diagnosis. She began working on the idea when she was pregnant; she now has two sons under the age of 4. “I personally experienced the pain point,” she said. “My child is screaming and sick, and the pediatrician’s office is closed because it’s 9 o’clock at night. From an entrepreneur’s perspective, there is nothing better than being an actual user.”
The fact that fewer women found start-ups around science and new technologies is a concern to nonprofits like the
Kauffman Foundation
and corporations like
3M
,
Merck
and
Dell
(and even the
White House
). When female perspectives are left out, innovations tend to be male-centric, often overlooking the needs or desires of women.
“When new companies and industries flourish, everyone benefits,” according to a Kauffman report,
“Overcoming the Gender Gap
.” “And the returns will increase when more women contribute to the process by bringing their ideas to market and building high-growth firms around them.”
Women who are pursuing start-ups in tech or science say they are often inspired to create products that they as consumers would use. In San Francisco, Leah Sparks and Katherine Bellevin are developing
Due Date Plus
, a smartphone-enabled maternity program. Surbhi Sarna of
nVision
, who suffered from ovarian cysts, is working on devices to detect ovarian cancer and tube blockages.
Barriers remain high, however. Most of the venture capitalists who finance start-ups in the STEM fields are men who don’t always understand or feel comfortable with women-centric technologies. Ms. Sarna, who has raised $4.5 million, said she stopped using the word “vagina” in her pitch, because it made men squirm. She didn’t have the same issue pitching to
Astia Angels
, a group that specializes in investing in women-led ventures.
Unlike many women, Ms. Sheng said she was encouraged at an early age to pursue science. Her father, who worked in laser technology, flew planes and taught her about the physics of flying. Her mother was a scientist who took Ms. Sheng along on trips on which she watched her mother present research findings at international conferences. Working in science and tech, she said, never seemed unusual “because I saw my mom doing that.”
Ms. Sheng, along with her co-founder, Erik Douglas, has raised $5.6 million for CellScope, which was spun out of a research lab at the University of California, Berkeley in 2011. Before joining the lab, Ms. Sheng helped design an artificial heart at
Abiomed
and a microscope for blood smears at
Medica
, both in the Boston area. After moving back to San Francisco, her hometown, to be closer to family, she heard about Berkeley’s research lab, which was designing a microscope for remote diagnoses of tuberculosis and malaria in developing nations. She took a pay cut to join the lab. “It was the riskier and more uncertain path,” she said, “but I was definitely more excited by it.”
After two years, Ms. Sheng and Mr. Douglas decided to license the lab’s technology and form CellScope to focus on health care issues closer to home. Ms. Sheng said they knew from talking to parents that children’s ear infections were a real concern. They have spent the last few years building a prototype for the otoscope, refining the design and signing up 800 doctors to use it. The doctors, she said, “were instrumental in helping us validate the quality of our product and providing feedback on how to improve it.”
CellScope, which now has 12 employees, plans a limited release in January of the Oto HOME to consumers in California, selling the otoscope and its related software for $79. After parents use the device for an ear exam, they can use the software to communicate with CellScope’s network of doctors. The fee will be $40 per remote diagnosis, she said.
The company also plans to sell
a professional version
, for $300, that doctors can use in their offices to show patients (or their parents) a digital video of the eardrum and explain diagnoses.
Ms. Sheng said the products would be sold directly from CellScope’s website, and the company has hired a business development manager to help widen distribution to retail shelves. Initially, the focus will be on parents of children who get three or more ear infections a year; she estimated that nearly five million children in the United States get chronic ear infections. The company plans to target these parents through social media, email campaigns and word-of-mouth marketing.
After years of refining the product’s technical design, Ms. Sheng said she was looking forward to tackling more business-related challenges. “Building something is one thing,” she said. “It’s another thing to figure out the model and how to monetize it.”
Colleen DeBaise is director of digital media for
The Story Exchange
, a nonprofit media organization dedicated to telling the stories of women who own businesses. You can follow it on
Twitter
.
Correction: November 13, 2014
An earlier version of this post misidentified the region of the ear that Ms. Sheng's device observes. It is the middle ear, not the inner ear.

Health workers have fought the Ebola outbreak to a tentative standstill in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous nation, offering at least a chance to eradicate the disease there before it spins out of control, as it has in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, where a sluggish response failed to halt it early.
Nigeria’s small number of cases — 11 confirmed and one suspected — provides a brief window in which to wipe out Ebola. If these efforts fail, the death toll could be horrific. The cases have occurred in Lagos, a city with 20 million people, many of them jammed into teeming slums where the virus could become unstoppable.
Dr. Thomas R. Frieden, the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said health officials were watching Nigeria with intense interest, because of its huge population and because it is much more of a crossroads than the other three countries, in much closer touch with the rest of Africa.
“We’re waiting for the other shoe to drop,” he said.
The World Health Organization
said on Thursday
that staff members on the front lines of the outbreak across the region had warned that the nearly 2,000 reported cases and the more than 1,000 reported deaths “vastly underestimate the magnitude of the outbreak.” And Doctors Without Borders said on Friday that the disease was still spreading faster than the efforts of governments and health workers to keep up with it, calling ground conditions “like a war.”
About 200 people who had contact with the infected patients in Lagos are receiving daily visits from health workers for 21 days, the incubation period of the disease, to check for fever or other symptoms, said David Daigle, a spokesman for the team in Nigeria from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. So far, 61 have finished the follow-up and are in the clear, he said. About 60 Nigerian health workers have been trained to trace contacts, and more are being taught, to bring the total to 200, Mr. Daigle said.
Ebola arrived in Nigeria on July 20, carried by Patrick Sawyer, a native Liberian and naturalized American citizen. He contracted the disease in Liberia, flew to Lagos while he was ill and died on July 25. Health officials say he was vomiting during the flight.
Every case in Nigeria has been traced to him. Some victims had helped him when he arrived at the airport, and others were health workers who had treated him without gloves or other protection because they did not realize he had Ebola. President Goodluck Jonathan has been widely quoted in Nigerian newspapers as calling Mr. Sawyer “a madman.”
Four Nigerian patients have died, and the mood among the rest is somber, said Dr. Maurizio Barbeschi, a scientist from the World Health Organization who is working on the outbreak.
“They think it is a death sentence,” he said. But he said they were getting good care, and he doubted that their death rate would reach that of the other countries, where about 60 percent of the cases have been fatal in some locations.

Patients who are health workers are caring for others, helping with tasks like changing bags of intravenous medicines.
Last Saturday, Dr. Barbeschi said, he stepped outside the ward where patients are being treated and asked if anyone had a book so he could read to the patients. Mr. Daigle pulled a beat-up copy of Shakespeare’s “Henry IV” from his backpack.
Back inside, speaking through a surgical mask, Dr. Barbeschi acted out scenes from the play for a patient fighting for his life.
Nigeria has some advantages over other West African countries in dealing with the disease: It has a better health system, and it was on alert for Ebola because the illness had struck the other nations first. Doctors detected it there before a large number of people fell ill. Dr. Frieden said that it took too long to isolate the first person infected from contact, but that the ability to respond had improved tremendously.
But Lagos is a huge city. The outbreaks in the other countries have mostly struck villages and towns.
“An Ebola outbreak in a dense urban setting is very different from what we know already,” said Dr. Benjamin J. Park, an infection control specialist from the C.D.C. who is working on the outbreak in Lagos.
Health officials are using social media, among other channels, to get information to health workers in Lagos — a difficult task because the city has thousands of health facilities, including clinics and small hospitals, Dr. Park said.
Dr. Park has been training health workers in how to protect themselves around potentially infected patients. Everyone wants the white Tyvek suits that have been widely photographed, he said, but he tries to convince them that because the disease is spread only by bodily fluids, the suits are needed only when patients are very ill with symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea.
If used, they must be removed carefully to avoid contact with secretions that may have splashed on the outside. “I say: ‘Imagine that you’re covered with paint or mud. How are you going to take this off without getting any on your skin?’ ” Dr. Park said.
Recruiting health professionals to fight Ebola there has proved challenging. On Wednesday in Lagos, a Nigerian doctor who answered a government call said he was not very worried about the risks. But he declined to give his name because he feared reprisals from the state authorities for talking to the news media, and he said he worried that he would be stigmatized if others learned that he was involved with Ebola. Though the government was offering the equivalent of $185 a day, a substantial sum in Nigeria, only a dozen or so people answered the call that day.
A nurse who did respond said he hoped to work on the outbreak by day and continue his regular job at a private hospital by night. He also requested anonymity, for the same reasons as the doctor. Working at the private hospital was riskier than working on the outbreak , he said.
“Here, you already know the risk you are facing, but back at the hospital, it’s dangerous because you can’t treat every patient as an Ebola risk,” the nurse said. While working on the outbreak, he would at least be given training and kits with protective gear.
But he added, holding a Bible, “It’s God that protects, not the kits.”

“
La Bare
” takes its title from the club it chronicles, a male strip joint in Dallas. The name proves unfortunately apt for a rambling, superficial documentary that straddles the line between exposé and infomercial. Directed by the actor Joe Manganiello (who was inspired by his role in Steven Soderbergh’s “
Magic Mike
,” set in the world of male revues), this celebratory film argues that male stripping is more strenuous than its female counterpart: It requires a full-fledged act and an athlete’s regimen. We learn a bit about the stagecraft, such as how audience volunteers are selected and why underpants with flies are forbidden.
The dancers — often identified only by their stage names, in a choice that makes the film seem guarded — vary in insight. Channing credits his interest in stripping to Mr. Soderbergh’s movie. J. D. hopes to return to the restaurant business. Cesar (his real name), a veteran of Afghanistan and Iraq, says ex-servicemen’s main options are to work as bodyguards, bouncers or cops. Several ensemble members grow emotional discussing the shooting death of a colleague, Ruben Riguero, in one of the few interludes that depart from self-congratulation.
“La Bare”
seldom shows the dancers’ lives outside of the club. (In this respect, the fictional “Magic Mike” seems richer than the documentary.) In one excursion, Randy Ricks, known as Master Blaster, who has performed at La Bare since 1979, receives injections and cryogenic treatment to maintain his physique. That’s the kind of behind-the-scenes detail worth preserving.
“La Bare” is rated R (Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian). Les thongs.
